newsitem.title: CANADA: Quebec's separatist premier battles foes in party.
newsitem.headline: Quebec's separatist premier battles foes in party.

text.p: Quebec's charismatic Premier Lucien Bouchard faced down strong opposition from within his separatist Parti Quebecois on Sunday but emerged weakened from the party's major policy convention.

A little more than a year after leading the separatist forces to near-victory in a referendum on Quebec sovereignty, Bouchard was forced to fight off a challenge from party hard-liners unhappy with the direction in which he was taking the independence movement.
On Saturday Bouchard and his Cabinet were rocked by a leadership review vote in which nearly a quarter of the 1,800 delegates gathered at the convention refused to support the leader.

The result threw the convention into disarray as Bouchard, by far the most popular politician in the French-speaking Canadian province, stormed out of the meeting amid rumors he would either resign or call a snap election.

But Bouchard returned on Sunday, and in a speech wrapping up the three-day convention, he called his 76.7 percent support in the leadership ballot a "baptism of fire." The vote result was the worst showing by a leader in the party's history.

Bouchard, who took over the party last January, warned the convention that if Quebec sovereignty was to be achieved by 2000, the party must become more united and project a more open image to the world.

"To win re-election and make Quebec a sovereign country, we must be more disciplined than in the past," said Bouchard, whose conciliatory tone did not mask a harsh message to the party's militant faction.
Hard-line separatists were upset with Bouchard's refusal to toughen language laws that restrict the use of English in Quebec. He does not support a return to French-only commerical signs.
There is also opposition in the party's social-democratic wing to aggressive spending cuts aimed at eliminating Quebec's C$3.9 billion ($2.9 billion) deficit by 2000.
Bouchard's cozy links with pro-Canada business leaders and current reluctance to push sovereignty aggressively have encouraged suspicions he is not a true separatist.

Public-sector unions and anti-poverty groups, among the staunchest supporters of the Parti Quebecois and separation, staged a huge rally outside the convention on Saturday in which 10,000 braved frigid conditions to protest planned spending cuts.
Bouchard, who was greeted on arrival at the convention on Sunday morning with a 15-minute standing ovation and hugs from well-wishers, moved immediately to reimpose his leadership on the party.

He went to a microphone to say the Parti Quebecois would not be able "to look at itself in the mirror" if the convention passed a resolution calling on the government to toughen language laws to stamp out bilingualism.
He indicated he would quit the party if the resolution passed, since it would require the government to override minority rights guaranteed in the Canadian and provincial charters of rights.

The convention supported Bouchard by soundly rejecting the resolution, but some of the premier's opponents insisted his problems were just beginning. Indeed, Bouchard emerged from the convention with a divided party as his government was preparing to impose harsh budget cuts over the opposition of its traditional allies.
"You will have more and more debate not only inside the party but in the society," Louis O'Neill, a former Quebec Cabinet minister, said.
